title: Genesis
intro: 40 days through the book of Genesis, from creation to Joseph, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Genesis means "origin," and in Hebrew the book is called Bereshit, "In the beginning," after its first word. It opens the Torah, the heart of Jewish scripture, and the whole Bible for Christians. Tradition names Moses as its author; many modern scholars think it was woven together from older sources. Starting today, 40 days through Genesis, one verse at a time.

The first words God speaks in the Bible, and light appears three days before the sun and moon. In Latin the phrase is "Fiat lux." Jews and Christians read these six days in different ways: some take them literally, while others read the chapter as theological truth told through the forms of its ancient world.

The high point of the creation account. "Man" here is the Hebrew adam, meaning humankind, male and female together. Many scholars note that ancient kings were sometimes called the image of a god; Genesis gives that title to every human being. Jewish and Christian thought have long seen this verse as a foundation for human dignity.

The end of the sixth day. Through the chapter God calls what he has made "good" six times, and here, after creating humans, "very good," the seventh. Seven, a number of completeness in the Bible, shapes the whole account. Even its first verse has exactly seven words in Hebrew.

God rests on the seventh day. The Hebrew verb for resting here, shavat, means to stop or cease, and it is the root of Shabbat, the Sabbath. Jews keep Shabbat as a day of rest from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. Most Christians gather for worship on Sunday instead, the day of Jesus' resurrection.

Chapter 2 tells creation again, closer up and in a different style. God shapes a man from the ground, like a potter, and breathes life into him. The Hebrew holds a pun: the man is adam, the ground is adamah. Written in capitals, "LORD" stands for God's personal name, YHWH, which Jews traditionally don't say aloud, reading Adonai, "Lord," instead.

For the first time in Genesis, something is "not good": the man is alone. The Hebrew word for helper, ezer, is used elsewhere in the Bible mostly of God himself, so it doesn't suggest someone lesser. God then forms the woman, and the man's words on seeing her, "bone of my bones," are the first human speech recorded in the Bible.

A serpent persuades the woman to eat from the forbidden tree, the man eats too, and they hide. This is the first question God asks in the Bible. The fruit is never named; the apple came later, perhaps from a Latin pun, since malum means both "apple" and "evil." Many Christians call this story "the Fall," while Jewish tradition generally reads it without the idea of inherited sin.

After God announces the consequences of their choice, the man gives his wife a name. In Hebrew she is Chavah, which sounds like the word for "living." Just after hearing that humans will return to dust, he names her for life. God then clothes them and sends them out of Eden, with cherubim guarding the way back to the tree of life.

Adam and Eve's sons: Cain farms, Abel keeps sheep. When God accepts Abel's offering but not his, Cain kills his brother in a field, the Bible's first murder. Abel's Hebrew name, Hevel, means "breath" or "vapor." Cain's evasive answer, "Am I my brother's keeper?", became a lasting phrase about responsibility for others.

Generations pass, and Genesis says violence filled the earth and God was grieved in his heart. Noah is the exception. There is wordplay in the Hebrew: the two letters of Noah's name, reversed, spell the word for favor, chen. God tells Noah to build an ark for his family and the animals.

After the flood, God makes a covenant, a binding promise, with Noah and every living creature: never again a flood to destroy the earth. The Hebrew word for rainbow, qeshet, is also the word for a warrior's bow. Ancient Mesopotamia had its own flood stories, such as the one in the Epic of Gilgamesh, and scholars have long compared them with this one.

People settle in Shinar, in Mesopotamia, and build a tower of baked brick to "make a name" for themselves. God scatters them by confusing their language. The place is called Babel, the Hebrew name for Babylon, which sounds like the Hebrew word for "confuse." Many scholars think the story recalls Mesopotamia's ziggurats, its stepped temple towers.

The story narrows from all humanity to one family. Abram had come with his father from Ur, usually identified with a city in what is now southern Iraq, to Haran. Now God calls him to leave his homeland and family, and he sets out at age 75. Jews, Christians, and Muslims all look to Abraham as a father of faith.

The rest of God's promise to Abram. Just before this, God says he will make Abram's name great, the very thing the builders of Babel tried to seize for themselves. Now the promise reaches past one family to "all the families of the earth." God repeats this promise to Isaac and to Jacob later in Genesis.

Abram is old and still childless, and he fears a servant will be his heir. God takes him outside under the night sky. "Credited" is a word for reckoning or counting, as if trust were entered in Abram's account. The apostle Paul later builds his teaching on faith around this verse, and Jewish tradition honors Abraham as a model of faithfulness.

Sarai, still childless, gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram, a practice known from other ancient Near Eastern texts. Mistreated by Sarai once she is pregnant, Hagar flees into the desert, where an angel tells her to name her son Ishmael, "God hears." Hagar, an enslaved foreigner, then gives God a name of her own: El Roi, "the God who sees me."

Thirteen years later, when Abram is 99, God renews the covenant. Abram, "exalted father," becomes Abraham, which the verse explains as "father of many nations," and Sarai becomes Sarah. Circumcision is given as the covenant's sign, and Jewish families still mark it on a baby boy's eighth day in a ceremony called the brit milah.

Three visitors arrive at Abraham's tent by the oaks of Mamre, and he rushes to feed them, a famous picture of hospitality. When one says Sarah will have a son, she laughs, since she is about 90. Jewish tradition generally sees the visitors as angels, while Andrei Rublev's famous Russian icon reads them as an image of the Christian Trinity.

God reveals that he is about to judge the wicked cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Abraham pushes back. He bargains like a trader: would God spare the city for 50 righteous people? For 45? He talks God down to ten. It is one of the Bible's boldest moments, a human being arguing with God for the sake of justice.

After 25 years of waiting since the first promise, Sarah gives birth to a son, and Abraham is 100. Abraham names him Isaac, in Hebrew Yitzchak, which means "he laughs." The laughter that once came from disbelief turns into laughter of joy, shared with everyone who hears the news.

One of the hardest stories in the Bible. God tests Abraham by telling him to offer Isaac as a sacrifice; at the last moment an angel stops him, and a ram is offered instead. In Judaism it is called the Akedah, "the binding," and it is read in synagogues at Rosh Hashanah. Many Christians see it as foreshadowing Jesus, the "Lamb of God."

posts.display: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you will be separated; one people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger.”
posts.caption: Isaac marries Rebekah, and after twenty years she becomes pregnant with twins who struggle inside her. This is God's answer when she asks why. The second twin is born gripping his brother's heel, so he is named Jacob, from the Hebrew word for heel. Again and again, Genesis favors a younger son over an older one.

Esau had already traded his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew. Now Isaac is old and nearly blind, and Rebekah helps Jacob disguise himself as Esau, with goatskins on his hands and neck, to take his father's blessing. Isaac is suspicious but blesses him anyway. Jacob's name sounds like a Hebrew verb for cheating, and Esau makes exactly that pun.

Fleeing his brother's anger, Jacob stops for the night with a stone for a pillow. He dreams of a ladder, or perhaps a stairway, connecting earth and heaven; the Hebrew word appears nowhere else in the Bible. At the top, God repeats the promise once given to Abraham. "Jacob's ladder" became the subject of a well-known African American spiritual.

Jacob wakes from his dream amazed. He had thought he was just stopping at "a certain place." He sets up his stone pillow as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel, "house of God." Bethel later became an important center of worship in ancient Israel.

Jacob reaches his mother's family and falls in love with his cousin Rachel at a well. He agrees to work seven years for her father, Laban. But on the wedding night Laban swaps in Rachel's older sister, Leah, and Jacob, who once deceived his own father, is deceived in turn. He works seven more years for Rachel.

Twenty years later, Jacob heads home to face Esau, who is coming with 400 men. The night before, alone by the Jabbok River, he wrestles a mysterious man until dawn and won't let go, even with a wounded hip. The prophet Hosea calls the man an angel; Jacob names the place Peniel, "face of God."

The stranger gives Jacob a new name, Israel, which the verse explains as one who has "struggled with God." The name passes to his twelve sons, the ancestors of Israel's twelve tribes, and much later to a nation. Jacob leaves limping, and Jewish dietary law still avoids the hip tendon of animals because of this story.

Jacob approaches Esau bowing to the ground seven times, expecting the worst. Instead, Esau runs to meet him, and the two brothers weep together. Many readers hear an echo of this scene in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son, where a father runs to embrace and kiss his returning son.

The last part of Genesis follows Joseph, Jacob's favorite son. The Hebrew words for his robe are uncertain, possibly a long robe with sleeves; "many colors" comes from the ancient Greek translation, and later inspired the musical Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat. The robe, and Joseph's dreams of his family bowing to him, turn his brothers' jealousy into hatred.

Joseph's brothers sell him to traders for twenty pieces of silver, and he becomes a slave in the house of Potiphar, an Egyptian officer. "The LORD was with Joseph" echoes through this chapter, even after Potiphar's wife falsely accuses him and he lands in prison. God never speaks to Joseph directly; instead the story shows God quietly at work behind the scenes.

After years in prison, Joseph is summoned to interpret Pharaoh's dreams: seven thin cows devouring seven fat ones, and withered grain swallowing full grain. He gives the credit to God and explains: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine. Pharaoh puts him over all Egypt at age 30, thirteen years after his brothers sold him.

The famine reaches Canaan, and Jacob sends ten of his sons to Egypt to buy grain. They bow before the governor, not realizing he is the brother they sold, now an Egyptian official speaking through an interpreter. Joseph's boyhood dream of his brothers' sheaves bowing to his has come true.

Joseph tests his brothers by planting his silver cup in the sack of Benjamin, the youngest, and threatening to keep him as a slave. Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph, now offers himself in Benjamin's place so their father won't lose another son. The word "Jew" comes from Judah's name, through his tribe and kingdom.

Judah's plea breaks Joseph. He sends his servants out and weeps so loudly that the Egyptians hear him. Then he tells his terrified brothers who he is, and goes further: God, he says, sent him ahead of them to save lives.

Joseph sends wagons to bring his father and the whole family to Egypt, and God tells Jacob in a vision not to be afraid to go. Jacob had believed for over twenty years that Joseph was dead. Father and son meet in the land of Goshen, and Joseph embraces him and weeps for a long time.

Joseph presents his father to Pharaoh, and it is the old shepherd who blesses the king. Jacob is 130, yet by his family's measure that is few: Abraham lived to 175 and Isaac to 180. Jacob's own years had included exile, deception, and long grief.

On his deathbed, Jacob speaks a poem over each of his twelve sons. To Judah he promises the scepter, a symbol of kingship, and Israel's great king David later came from this tribe. "Shiloh" is a puzzling word that translations render in different ways, and ancient Jewish interpreters and Christians alike read the line as pointing to the Messiah.

After Jacob dies, Joseph's brothers fear he has only been waiting to take revenge. Instead he forgives them, and this line sums up the whole Joseph story. Genesis ends with the family settled in Egypt, setting the stage for the book of Exodus. That's the whole of Genesis. Thank you for reading it with me.
